thread.title: NYYC seeks to preserve America's Cup
thread.title_full: NYYC seeks to preserve America's Cup

author: ohtadmin
title: NYYC seeks to preserve America's Cup
text:
The New York Yacht Club is asking whether the newly created America’s Cup Partnership can be reconciled with the Deed of Gift, which is the 1887 charitable trust that has governed the cup since the 19th century.
The club’s commodore, Clare Harrington, made the announcement Monday after she requested New York’s attorney general to review the partnership. The yacht club has clubhouses in Newport and New York City.
“The America’s Cup has endured for more than 170 years because the Deed of Gift provides a durable, legal framework that cannot simply be reorganized at will,” she said.
The yacht club wants to know whether the America’s Cup remains, in the words of the deed, a “perpetual challenge cup for friendly competition between foreign countries,” or whether it can be converted into “a centrally managed, commercially controlled regatta run by a standing body of incumbent competitors.”
The Auld Mug was won by the schooner America in 1851 and given, by the Deed of Gift, to the yacht in 1857 to be held in trust as an international challenge trophy. The club that holds the cup, under the deed, serves as its trustee. The terms of each match are agreed cycle by cycle, by mutual consent, between that club, referred to as the defender, and the first qualifying challenger, referred to as the challenger of record.
The yacht club notes that this deliberately narrow, two-party structure — renewed each cycle by whichever clubs then hold and challenge for the cup — has defined the event for more than a century, and the deed has been altered only a handful of times, each time by order of the New York courts.
The yacht club contends the America’s Cup Partnership — established under the protocol for the 38th America’s Cup and a purported set of related “partnership agreements” that have not been made public — departs from that structure in fundamental respects.
The yacht club said a permanent authority is something the deed has never contemplated. The America’s Cup Partnership, however, is designed to govern the organization, rules and commercial rights of all future America’s Cups, regardless of which clubs has or challenges for the cup.
That yacht club contends the deed vests governance in the defender and challenger of record of each cycle and does not authorize any standing body apart from them.
The yacht club also believes the partnership presents a potential barrier to the right to challenge. Under Article 13.1 of the protocol, a qualified club that declines to join the partnership may have its challenge rejected absent the unanimous approval of the partnership’s board. The yacht club says this “subordinates a right the deed grants freely to any qualifying club to the discretion of a private body made up of existing competitors.”
The partnership also sets rules for matches not yet challenged. The yacht club says that a body purporting to fix the terms of future matches — between clubs not yet identified —displaces the mutual consent mechanism the deed requires.
The yacht club said there is a lack of transparency through the partnership. A “restructuring of this magnitude” has proceeded without disclosure of the partnership agreements to interested yacht clubs or the attorney general and without the judicial approval.
The yacht club also is concerned about “a potential change in the essential purpose of the trust” by transforming the America’s Cup from an open challenge into a periodic, centrally organized regatta. This is an alteration of the trust’s charitable purpose that, in the club’s view, cannot be made without modification of the deed and approval of the New York courts.
“We hold the deepest respect for the competition and for every club that has held the cup,” Harrington said. “Precisely because of that respect, we believe these questions deserve careful review under New York law so that whatever governance the cup carries forward rests on a sound legal foundation and preserves the open challenge that makes the cup what it is.”
Harrington emphasized that the club’s concerns are directed at the legal structure of the America’s Cup Partnership and the process by which it was adopted, not at the sportsmanship of any competitor.
“We are asking the attorney general’s charities bureau to review the trustee’s administration of the trust and to obtain the undisclosed partnership agreements for examination,” Harrington said.
The club has asked the charities bureau to consider whether the structure is consistent with the rights and obligations established by the deed and whether further action or judicial review may be appropriate.
summary: The yacht club wants to know whether the America’s Cup remains, in the words of the deed, a “perpetual challenge cup for friendly competition between foreign countries,” or whether it can be converted into “a centrally managed, commercially controlled regatta run by a standing body of incumbent competitors.” The Auld Mug was won by the schooner America in 1851 and given, by the Deed of Gift, to the yacht in 1857 to be held in trust as an international challenge trophy.
